title: The skeptics
hookLine: Pyrrho's followers suspended judgment and found calm in not deciding

lines: A PAINTER, A HORSE, THE FOAM.
PEACE ARRIVES WHEN YOU STOP GRABBING.
cards: A painter is trying to paint a horse, and he can't get the foam at its mouth right. He tries and tries. Finally, furious, he throws his sponge at the canvas.
Where it hits, it leaves a mark, and the mark looks exactly like foam.

The story was told by an ancient doctor and philosopher named Sextus Empiricus, to explain something odd: how peace of mind arrived for his school the moment they stopped trying to grab it. Today: the skeptics.

teach.b: First, the founder. Pyrrho of Elis lived around the time of Alexander the Great and, according to Diogenes Laërtius, traveled with Alexander's army as far as India, where he met local sages. He wrote nothing.

Later followers took his name: Pyrrhonists. Wild stories were told about him, that friends had to pull him out of the way of carts because he wouldn't trust his senses. Even some ancient writers doubted those.
Second, the method. The skeptics noticed that for almost any claim, you can find an argument against it that seems just as strong. Is honey sweet?
To you, yes; to someone sick, bitter.
So they practiced epochē: suspending judgment, holding off from saying how things really are. Not denying. Just not deciding.
Third, the surprise. Sextus says that, like the painter, the skeptics had hoped to find calm by figuring out the truth. They couldn't settle it.
So they suspended judgment, and calm followed, as a shadow follows a body. Like the sponge, it came when they stopped forcing it. Fourth, how they lived.
They followed appearances, custom, their own needs, the rules of their craft.
They ate when hungry and lived by local ways, without insisting those ways were the final truth. The Stoics thought certainty was possible and worth working for. The skeptics found peace without it.
Both were looking for an untroubled mind.

how: Pyrrhonian skeptics practiced suspending judgment, weighing opposing arguments until they balanced, and living by appearances and custom without claiming final truth.

games.q: you're the painter, and you can't paint the horse's foam no matter what you try. what happens in the story?
o: you keep trying until you get it right.
you throw the sponge in frustration, and it makes the foam.
games.why: the sponge made the foam by accident. Sextus says calm came to the skeptics the same way, once they stopped forcing an answer.

practice: Think of one judgment you're holding tightly, about someone's motives, about how something will turn out, about who's right, and find the best honest case for the opposite. Then, instead of choosing, say: I'm not sure.
Notice what happens in your body when you stop gripping the answer.

wordCard.voice: The skeptics. Pyrrho's followers suspended judgment, and found that calm followed when they stopped insisting on an answer. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a holding back, suspension of judgment. The skeptics' central practice.

carryVoice: Your line: I'm not sure. The skeptics left that short phrase, worth keeping close in any argument. Until tomorrow.

sources.work: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers
